overview: This unit covers predicate logic (Prädikatlogik), logical connectives (Junktoren), quantifiers (Quantoren), and valid inferences. Truth tables and diagrams help evaluate compound statements; bounded quantifiers express claims about selected objects. Examples involving syllogisms, systems of equations, and forms of inference show how to assess conclusions and refute invalid arguments with countermodels. Direct proof, contraposition, proof by contradiction, and equivalence proof are central strategies; induction is also mentioned.

entries.short: Predicate logic describes properties of objects and relations between them using variables and quantifiers.
entries.explanation: In predicate logic, statements can depend on which objects are assigned to variables. Predicates express properties or relations, and quantifiers state whether something holds for every object or for at least one object. This makes it possible to formulate general claims that go beyond individual, fully specified statements.
entries.example: With the integers as the domain and predicates G(x) for “x is even” and Z(x) for “x is an integer,” ∀x (G(x) ⇒ Z(x)) expresses that every even integer is an integer.
pitfalls: An open formula with a free variable has no definite truth value until the variable is assigned a value.
entries.heading: 1. Prädikatlogik und Aussageformen

entries.short: A predicate is an open formula whose truth value depends on the objects assigned to its variables.
entries.explanation: An open formula such as “x is an integer” contains a variable and receives a definite truth value only after an assignment. A predicate can also contain several variables and thereby express a relation between objects. Variables can be assigned specific objects or bound by quantifiers.
entries.example: For P(x) = “x is even,” P(4) is true and P(5) is false.
pitfalls: An open formula is not automatically true or false while its free variables remain unassigned.
entries.heading: 1. Prädikatlogik und Aussageformen

entries.short: The domain specifies which objects variables may denote; quantifiers bind variables.
entries.explanation: The domain and the meanings of the predicates must be specified in order to evaluate a formula. A variable is free if no quantifier binds it; free variables must be assigned values to determine the truth value of the open formula. A bound variable lies within the scope of a quantifier such as ∀ or ∃.
entries.example: √2 is a permissible assignment for a variable whose domain is ℝ, but not for a variable whose domain is ℚ.
pitfalls: A statement can change its truth value when the domain changes.
A formula can contain bound and free variables at the same time.
entries.heading: 1. Prädikatlogik und Aussageformen

entries.short: Logical connectives combine statements, and a truth table shows the result for every possible assignment.
entries.explanation: The logical connectives include negation ¬A, conjunction A ∧ B, disjunction A ∨ B, conditional A ⇒ B, and biconditional A ⇔ B. In the lecture notes, w denotes “true” and f denotes “false.” The OR is inclusive, so it is true when at least one component statement is true; a truth table systematically lists all assignments.
entries.example: For A = f and B = w, A ∨ B = w and A ⇔ B = f.
pitfalls: Logical OR is inclusive unless exclusive OR is explicitly intended.
For ¬A, the truth value of another statement B does not affect the result.
entries.heading: 2. Junktoren und ihre Wahrheitsbereiche

entries.short: Exclusive OR is true exactly when one of two statements is true.
entries.explanation: “Either A or B” in its usual exclusive sense denotes a connective that is false when both statements have the same truth value. It is true when one statement is true and the other is false. It can be expressed, for example, by (A ∧ ¬B) ∨ (¬A ∧ B).
entries.example: If A = f and B = w, exclusive OR is true; if A = w and B = w, it is false.
pitfalls: Inclusive OR A ∨ B is also true when both component statements are true.
entries.heading: 2. Junktoren und ihre Wahrheitsbereiche

entries.short: The conditional A ⇒ B is false exactly when A is true and B is false.
entries.explanation: A ⇒ B is read as “if A, then B.” If A is true, B must also be true; if A is false, the conditional is true regardless of B. In propositional logic, it specifies a truth condition, not causation or temporal order.
entries.example: “If pigs can fly, then π is irrational” is true when its antecedent is false.
pitfalls: A false antecedent does not make the conditional false.
A conditional by itself does not assert a substantive connection between its antecedent and consequent.
entries.heading: Konditional und Bikonditional

entries.short: A ⇔ B is true when A and B have the same truth value.
entries.explanation: A ⇔ B is read as “A if and only if B.” The biconditional is equivalent to the conjunction of both directions: (A ⇒ B) ∧ (B ⇒ A). It therefore requires both that B follows from A and that A follows from B.
entries.example: For real x, x + 2 = 5 ⇔ x = 3.
pitfalls: Showing only one of the two implication directions is not enough to establish a biconditional.
related: If and only if and logical equivalence
entries.heading: Konditional und Bikonditional

entries.short: The if-then-else connective returns the truth value of B when A is true and of C when A is false.
entries.explanation: For “if A, then B, else C,” I(A,B,C) ≡ (A ∧ B) ∨ (¬A ∧ C). An equivalent form is I(A,B,C) ≡ (A ⇒ B) ∧ (¬A ⇒ C). The special form “if A, then B, else true” corresponds to A ⇒ B; “if A, then B, else not B” corresponds to A ⇔ B.
entries.example: For A = f, B = w, and C = f, the result is false because when A is false, the else branch C determines the result.
pitfalls: When A is false, C determines the result; B is then irrelevant.
related: Difference from branching in a program
entries.heading: If-Then-Else als logische Verknüpfung

entries.term: Matching truth regions to Venn diagrams
entries.short: To check a diagram for a logical statement, evaluate its regions as assignments of truth values to the statements.
entries.explanation: Each region represents a combination in which A, B, and, where applicable, C are true or false. Read off those truth values for a region, evaluate the formula using the corresponding table row, and compare the result with the region’s color. Repeat for the remaining regions. For a conditional, only A ∧ ¬B is false; a general if-then-else can be false for several combinations.
entries.example: For A ⇒ B, the part inside A and outside B is the only false region.
pitfalls: In a diagram with three statements, one region can combine several table rows if one statement is irrelevant to the formula.
entries.heading: Ein Venn-Diagramm einer Aussage zuordnen

entries.term: Difference from branching in a program
entries.short: A logical if-then-else combines truth values, while a program executes instructions depending on a condition.
entries.explanation: In a programming language, a condition A usually precedes a branch. The branches contain instructions that are executed depending on the condition’s truth value. By contrast, the logical connective evaluates the truth values of A, B, and C and itself returns a truth value.
entries.example: In Python, `if A: print("b") else: print("c")` executes one of the two instructions depending on A.
pitfalls: Instructions in program branches are not themselves automatically the truth values B and C in a logical formula.
entries.heading: Unterschied zur Verzweigung im Programm

entries.short: A propositional formula is universally valid if it is true under every assignment.
entries.explanation: Universal validity means that no possible assignment of the statements in the formula makes it false. A formula A ⇒ B is not universally valid merely by its form, since it is false when A = w and B = f. For open formulas, the domain of objects under consideration must also be specified.
entries.example: A ∨ ¬A is true under every assignment.
pitfalls: A single true assignment is not enough to establish universal validity.
Universal validity of a formula and validity of an inference are related but distinct concepts.
entries.heading: 3. Gültigkeit, hinreichende und notwendige Bedingungen

entries.short: If A ⇒ B holds, A is sufficient for B and B is necessary for A.
entries.explanation: A is sufficient for B if A is enough to infer B. B is necessary for A if A cannot hold without B. In set-theoretic terms, the truth set of A is then contained in the truth set of B: {x | A(x)} ⊆ {x | B(x)}. If both directions hold, each statement is necessary and sufficient for the other.
entries.example: For real x, “x/2 is an integer” is sufficient for “x is an integer”; x being an integer is necessary for x/2 to be an integer.
pitfalls: For A ⇒ B, A is sufficient and B is necessary; reversing the direction swaps these roles.
entries.heading: Allgemeine Begriffe

entries.term: If and only if and logical equivalence
entries.short: “Iff” means “if and only if,” and logically equivalent open formulas have the same truth value under every assignment.
entries.explanation: “A iff B” denotes the biconditional A ⇔ B. Two open formulas are logically equivalent if their truth values agree under all assignments. The lecture notes use “GDW” to mark an equivalence and “syn” for synonymy or equivalence.
entries.example: A ⇔ B and (A ⇒ B) ∧ (B ⇒ A) are logically equivalent.
pitfalls: Equivalence requires agreement under all assignments, not just in one example.
entries.heading: „gdw“, „GDW“ und gleichbedeutende Aussageformen

entries.short: A mathematical theorem or lemma is a claim whose validity must be proved under specified assumptions.
entries.explanation: A theorem is a mathematical claim, often in the form “if A, then B.” A lemma is also a claim to be proved and often serves as an intermediate step in another proof. The claim holds within its specified domain and under its assumptions.
entries.example: For real x, the claim x/2 ∈ ℤ ⇒ x ∈ ℤ is a conditional whose validity must be justified in the stated domain.
pitfalls: The form “A implies B” is not automatically true for arbitrary meanings of A and B.
entries.heading: Allgemeine Begriffe

entries.short: A bounded quantifier states a claim only about objects that satisfy a specified restriction.
entries.explanation: The universal quantifier ∀ means “for all,” and the existential quantifier ∃ means “there is at least one.” “All objects satisfying R satisfy P” means ∀x (R(x) ⇒ P(x)); R is the restriction and P is the required property. A bounded existential claim can be expressed, for example, as ∃x (R(x) ∧ P(x)).
entries.example: “Every integer divisible by 4 is even” can be written as ∀x (D₄(x) ⇒ G(x)) when the domain is ℤ.
pitfalls: “Some” means at least one object and does not rule out additional objects with the property.
A universal statement does not claim that any object satisfies the restriction.
entries.heading: Alle Objekte mit R haben auch P

entries.short: The four forms state whether all, not all, some, or no objects satisfying R have property P.
entries.explanation: “All R are P” means ∀x (R(x) ⇒ P(x)); “not all R are P” means ∃x (R(x) ∧ ¬P(x)). “Some R are P” means ∃x (R(x) ∧ P(x)); “no R is P” means ∀x (R(x) ⇒ ¬P(x)). A dot in a quantifier diagram marks an asserted witness, while a shaded region is empty or excluded.
entries.example: “Some positive real numbers have square 4” is true because x = 2 has both properties.
pitfalls: “Not all R are P” means that at least one R is not P; it does not mean that no R is P.
entries.heading: Die vier wichtigen Formen

entries.short: Venn diagrams show all combinations of membership, while Euler diagrams represent specific relationships between sets.
entries.explanation: A Venn diagram divides the objects under consideration into regions for every combination of membership and non-membership in the sets. An Euler diagram represents specific relationships between sets through the positions of its curves, for example by placing one circle entirely inside another. In quantifier diagrams, a shaded region can be marked as empty or excluded.
entries.example: If every A-object is also a B-object, an Euler diagram can show circle A entirely inside circle B.
pitfalls: A Venn diagram also shows combinations that must be empty because of a specific relationship between sets.
In everyday use, “Venn diagram” is sometimes used as a general term for set diagrams.
related: Matching truth regions to Venn diagrams
entries.heading: Venn- und Euler-Diagramme

entries.short: A witness satisfies an existential claim, and a counterexample refutes a universal claim.
entries.explanation: A witness is an object that satisfies the property asserted by an existential claim. A counterexample violates a universal claim and is also a witness for its negation. An existential claim can be proved with a suitable witness; a universal claim requires a general argument covering all objects under consideration.
entries.example: The number 1 is a counterexample to “All integers are even,” since 1 is an integer and is odd.
pitfalls: A suitable example generally does not prove a universal claim.
One unsuccessful candidate does not refute an existential claim.
entries.heading: Zeugen und Gegenbeispiele

entries.short: When negating a quantifier, “for all” becomes “there exists,” and the property is negated.
entries.explanation: We have ¬∀x P(x) ≡ ∃x ¬P(x) and ¬∃x P(x) ≡ ∀x ¬P(x). It follows as well that ∀x P(x) ≡ ¬∃x ¬P(x) and ∃x P(x) ≡ ¬∀x ¬P(x). Thus, the negation of a universal claim says that at least one counterexample exists.
entries.example: “Not all integers are even” means “There is an integer that is not even.”
pitfalls: When negating a quantifier, both the quantifier and the property must be negated.
entries.heading: Quantoren durch Negation ausdrücken

entries.short: The truth value of a quantified statement can depend on whether its domain is ℚ or ℝ.
entries.explanation: The rational numbers ℚ are a subset of the real numbers ℝ, and some real numbers are not rational. Therefore, the same property can have different truth values over ℚ and ℝ. For example, x² ≠ 2 holds for all rational x, but not for all real x, since √2 is real and its square is 2.
entries.example: ∃x ∈ ℚ: x² = 2 is false, whereas ∃x ∈ ℝ: x² = 2 is true.
pitfalls: √2 is not a permissible witness for an existential claim whose domain is ℚ.
entries.heading: Rationale und reelle Zahlen unterscheiden

entries.short: A conditional specifies which antecedent leads to the consequent; the reverse direction must be checked separately.
entries.explanation: A ⇒ B and B ⇒ A are generally not equivalent. For real x, x = √2 ⇒ x² = 2, but the converse must account for both solutions: x² = 2 ⇒ (x = −√2 ∨ x = √2). Swapping the antecedent and consequent can therefore produce a false statement.
entries.example: “x is a solution of x² = 2” does not imply that x = √2, since x = −√2 is also a solution.
pitfalls: The converse of a true conditional is not automatically true.
entries.heading: Die Richtung eines Konditionals beachten

entries.short: A syllogism is an inference in which a conclusion is derived from premises.
entries.explanation: In its classical Aristotelian form, a syllogism has exactly two premises and one conclusion, often using statements of the forms “all,” “some,” or “no.” Validity depends on the structure of the inference, not on whether the names used refer to real objects. An inference is valid if true premises cannot lead to a false conclusion.
entries.example: All Bandersnatches are Borogoves; all Borogoves are slithy; therefore, all Bandersnatches are slithy.
pitfalls: The truth of the conclusion alone does not show that it follows from the premises.
entries.heading: 5. Syllogismen und gültige Schlussfolgerungen

entries.short: An inference is valid if there is no assignment under which all premises are true and the conclusion is false.
entries.explanation: Validity describes the logical relationship between premises and conclusion. It does not guarantee that the premises are actually true; it guarantees that the conclusion must be true if all the premises are true. An inference is invalid as soon as a countermodel exists in which the premises are true and the conclusion is false.
entries.example: “All pigs can fly” and “Miss Piggy is a pig” validly imply “Miss Piggy can fly,” even though the first premise is actually false.
pitfalls: Invalidity does not mean that the conclusion is always false; it means only that the conclusion does not necessarily follow from the premises.
The validity of an inference is not the same as the universal validity of a formula.
entries.heading: 5. Syllogismen und gültige Schlussfolgerungen

entries.short: Premises are the assumed starting statements of an inference, and the conclusion is the statement derived from them.
entries.explanation: An inference with premises P₁ and P₂ and conclusion C can be written as a fraction, with P₁ and P₂ above a horizontal line and C below it. This notation makes the structure of an inference visible. By itself, it does not establish whether the inference is valid.
entries.example: (A ⇒ B, A) above the inference line and B below it represents modus ponens.
pitfalls: Simply writing a conclusion below a line does not prove that the inference rule is valid.
related: Modus ponens, modus tollens, and chaining conditionals
entries.heading: Prämissen und Konklusion

entries.short: The pig examples show that an inference’s validity depends on its logical form.
entries.explanation: “All pigs can fly” and “Miss Piggy is a pig” validly imply that Miss Piggy can fly. This does not follow from “Some pigs can fly” and “Miss Piggy is a pig,” since the flying pig could be a different one. By contrast, “Some pigs can fly” and “All pigs are animals” imply that some animals can fly.
entries.example: A countermodel to the invalid inference contains a flying pig d and a non-flying Miss Piggy.
pitfalls: “Some pigs can fly” does not mean that every pig can fly.
entries.heading: Schweine, Fliegen und Miss Piggy

entries.short: The examples about children distinguish valid inferences from converses that admit countermodels.
entries.explanation: If all children who behave well receive a gift, and Lea behaves well, it follows that Lea receives a gift. If some children behave well and all well-behaved children receive a gift, it follows that some children receive a gift. A gift for Lea does not imply that she behaved well; likewise, “Some well-behaved children receive gifts” and “Lea behaves well” do not imply that Lea receives a gift.
entries.example: For the invalid inference from Lea receiving a gift to her behaving well, Lea could receive a gift even though she did not behave well.
pitfalls: A general rule about a group does not automatically establish that every member of the group has the stated property.
entries.heading: Vier eigene Beispiele: Kinder, Benehmen und Geschenke

entries.term: Inferences in a system of linear equations
entries.short: In the elimination method, equations are multiplied and added so that one variable cancels.
entries.explanation: For 3x + 4y = 0 and −2x + 3y = 17, you can multiply the first equation by 2 and the second by 3. Adding them gives 17y = 51, so y = 3; substituting into the first equation gives x = −4. Checking both equations confirms the solution, and the derivation shows that every common solution pair must have these values.
entries.example: (x, y) = (−4, 3) satisfies both equations: 3(−4) + 4(3) = 0 and −2(−4) + 3(3) = 17.
pitfalls: A transformation must be applied to both sides of the equation.
A solution found should be checked in every original equation.
entries.heading: 6. Schlussfolgerungen bei einem linearen Gleichungssystem

entries.term: Modus ponens, modus tollens, and chaining conditionals
entries.short: Modus ponens, modus tollens, and chaining conditionals are valid forms of inference.
entries.explanation: Modus ponens has the form: from A ⇒ B and A, infer B. Modus tollens has the form: from A ⇒ B and ¬B, infer ¬A. For chaining conditionals, A ⇒ B and B ⇒ C imply A ⇒ C.
entries.example: If a code is accepted, access is granted; if access is granted, a confirmation appears; therefore, an accepted code leads to a confirmation.
pitfalls: Modus tollens requires ¬B as the second premise.
Swapping the antecedent and consequent is not one of these valid rules.
entries.heading: 7. Quantorenfreie Schlussformen

entries.short: A countermodel to an inference makes all its premises true and its conclusion false.
entries.explanation: To show that a form of inference is invalid, it is enough to give an assignment under which all the premises are true and the conclusion is false. For example, A ⇒ B and B do not necessarily imply A: when A = f and B = w, both premises are true, but the conclusion A is false. This assignment refutes the claimed validity.
entries.example: In the gift example, Lea can receive a gift without having behaved well.
pitfalls: A case with a false premise does not refute the validity of an inference.
entries.heading: Ein Gegenbeispiel entlarvt einen ungültigen Schluss

entries.short: Proof strategies provide systematic ways to justify a mathematical claim.
entries.explanation: In a direct proof, you derive the claim immediately from the assumption. In a proof by contraposition, you prove the equivalent statement ¬B ⇒ ¬A; in a proof by contradiction, you assume the negation of the claim and derive a contradiction. To prove a biconditional, show both directions or a chain of equivalent statements. Induction is mentioned as another strategy.
entries.example: To prove A ⇔ B, show A ⇒ B and B ⇒ A.
pitfalls: A proof strategy does not replace justification of each logical step.
Induction is only mentioned as a strategy in this unit; no method or example is provided.
entries.heading: 8. Übliche Beweisstrategien

entries.short: For a direct proof of A ⇒ B, assume A and derive B from it.
entries.explanation: The proof begins with the assumption and uses definitions, known facts, and valid transformations until the claim follows. For 0 ≤ x ≤ 2, x, 2 − x, and 2 + x are nonnegative. Therefore, −x³ + 4x + 1 = x(2 − x)(2 + x) + 1 ≥ 1 > 0, which proves the inequality for every x in the interval.
pitfalls: The assumption must not be silently replaced with a stronger one.
entries.heading: Direkter Beweis: eine Ungleichung

entries.short: A ⇒ B is logically equivalent to ¬B ⇒ ¬A.
entries.explanation: In a proof by contraposition, instead of proving the original implication, you prove “If B does not hold, then A does not hold.” For universal claims, the corresponding equivalence is ∀x (P(x) ⇒ Q(x)) ⇔ ∀x (¬Q(x) ⇒ ¬P(x)). For integers n, contraposing “If 3n + 2 is odd, then n is odd” gives: if n = 2k is even, then 3n + 2 = 2(3k + 1) is even.
entries.example: From “n even ⇒ 3n + 2 even,” contraposition gives “3n + 2 odd ⇒ n odd.”
pitfalls: Contraposition negates both statements and swaps their roles; simply swapping them is not contraposition.
related: Modus ponens, modus tollens, and chaining conditionals
entries.heading: Kontraposition

entries.short: In a proof by contradiction, assume the negation of the claim and derive a contradiction.
entries.explanation: To prove a statement A, assume ¬A and show that this leads to a contradiction. To prove “If 3n + 2 is odd, then n is odd,” you can assume n is even and write n = 2k. Then 3n + 2 = 2(3k + 1) is even, contradicting the assumption that it is odd.
entries.example: Assuming that n is even, together with 3n + 2 being odd, leads to the same expression being even.
pitfalls: The contradiction must be derived from the assumed negation and the available assumptions.
entries.heading: Widerspruch

entries.short: To prove A ⇔ B, show both implications or transform the statements into one another using valid steps.
entries.explanation: A biconditional holds exactly when both A ⇒ B and B ⇒ A hold. You can prove the two directions separately or provide a sequence of transformations that are valid in each direction. This shows that the statements have the same truth value or the same solutions.
entries.example: For real x, x + 2 = 5 ⇔ x = 3, since the equation can be transformed in both directions by adding or subtracting 2.
pitfalls: A transformation that preserves only one direction is not enough to establish an equivalence.
related: If and only if and logical equivalence
entries.heading: Äquivalenz beweisen

entries.short: Induction is mentioned in this unit as another proof strategy.
entries.explanation: The lecture notes list induction as a strategy, but provide neither a developed method nor an example here. Thus, this unit only records that induction is one of the common proof strategies.
pitfalls: This section of the unit does not explain any induction steps.
entries.heading: Induktion
